profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for the first two-week requirements phase of an AI-assisted support-ticket triage feature for a B2B SaaS platform. The company wants to tailor its normal requirements process for an ML-based capability, so the meeting focuses on how to produce an initial requirements package, what historical ticket sample will be used for discovery and labeling discussions, what prior artifacts can be reused, and when to bring architecture, legal, and support operations into review. The agenda is to define the planning work for the phase, assign owners, and agree on the timeline to a stakeholder review. The expected outcome is a concrete plan for producing the baseline requirements package, preparing the historical sample, reusing prior taxonomy work, and scheduling the review milestone.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Requirements discovery, enterprise workflow products, cross-functional planning for AI features
members.background: Former business analyst who now leads early-phase product definition for customer-facing AI capabilities in the support organization
members.private_state: She wants a clean, reviewable package quickly so she can show executives that the AI initiative is moving with a disciplined requirements approach without opening a long debate about process overhead.
hidden_assumptions: A 'baseline requirements' package is an initial, reviewable draft that frames goals, user scenarios, and open questions rather than a frozen specification.
A '200-ticket sample' means 200 total historical tickets chosen to be broadly representative enough for workshops and discussion.
A package is 'ready for stakeholder review' when it is coherent enough to prompt feedback, even if many details are still unresolved.
The 'pilot taxonomy' refers to the routing categories used in last quarter's support-operations discovery pilot.
Reusing prior artifacts mainly means borrowing structure and language, not inheriting strict governance or modeling conventions from engineering experiments.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: NLP systems, data pipelines, annotation workflows, operationalizing AI features inside production platforms
members.background: Former data engineer who now leads ML implementation planning and usually starts translating product discussions into data preparation and feasibility work immediately
members.private_state: He wants enough stability to begin annotation and feasibility work early, and he is trying to avoid another AI project where vague requirements caused repeated relabeling and rework.
hidden_assumptions: A 'baseline requirements' package is the minimum stable set of constraints and use-case boundaries needed to start data prep without likely rework.
A '200-ticket sample' means roughly 200 usable tickets per major queue or category after filtering, because a single pooled set would not support reliable annotation calibration.
Something is 'ready for stakeholder review' when the main ambiguities have already been resolved enough that stakeholders can effectively confirm rather than explore.
The 'pilot taxonomy' refers to the label schema used in the prior ML proof-of-concept for support-text classification.
When prior artifacts are reused in AI planning, they should be carried forward in a form that can plug directly into annotation and traceability work.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to deliver the baseline requirements by next Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an initial draft package with goals, key scenarios, constraints, and open questions that is suitable for discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a sufficiently settled set of requirements and boundaries that engineering can safely start annotation guidance and feasibility work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In planning meetings, 'baseline' sounds like a normal shared milestone, and both participants treat it as obviously desirable without spelling out whether it is exploratory or stable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that a 200-ticket sample will support the next phase.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 200 tickets total across the relevant support queues, enough to illustrate patterns and edge cases during requirements workshops.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means about 200 valid tickets for each major queue or label bucket after exclusions, because the sample must also support annotation calibration and feasibility checks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds specific and concrete, so it creates false confidence; neither participant feels a need to unpack whether the number is global or per subgroup.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to take the package to stakeholder review once it is ready.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready enough for architecture, legal, and support operations to react to the framing, expose gaps, and help shape the requirements.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready enough that those groups can mostly validate the package in one pass, with only minor adjustments remaining.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Review readiness is a second-order milestone criterion that teams often leave implicit, especially when everyone assumes they are simply being efficient and collaborative.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to reuse the pilot taxonomy to save time.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the support-operations routing taxonomy from the previous manual triage discovery pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the ML labeling taxonomy from the earlier text-classification proof of concept.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts came from recent internal 'pilot' work on support tickets, and the shorthand 'pilot taxonomy' feels familiar enough that neither notices they are indexing different documents.

turns.inner_thought: I need this first phase to produce a clean package quickly so I can show the exec team we have a disciplined requirements motion without getting dragged into a long methodology debate. By baseline requirements, I mean an initial draft that frames the problem well: goals, key user scenarios, likely failure modes, and the open questions we want architecture, legal, and support ops to react to. If I can get that into stakeholder review early next week, that is a win even if plenty is still unresolved.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. For this two-week phase, I'd like us to get the baseline requirements package together by next Friday and aim to take the package to stakeholder review once it is ready, ideally early next week. Today I want to lock the work plan, owners, and what we need in parallel so we don't lose momentum.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if baseline requirements land by Friday and are actually stable enough, I can get my team moving on annotation guidance and feasibility instead of waiting for another round of churn. I'll line up what I need under that milestone: roughly 200 usable tickets per major queue after filtering, and I'll reuse the pilot taxonomy from the earlier ML classification POC so we have a label structure that can flow into traceability work. That should give the baseline some concrete footing.
turns.utterance: That works for me. In parallel, I can prepare the 200-ticket sample and reuse the pilot taxonomy so we have something concrete sitting behind the baseline requirements. That should help keep the phase practical instead of purely conceptual.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. A pooled set of 200 historical tickets should be plenty to illustrate the main support flows, edge cases, and the kinds of handoffs people care about in discovery sessions. I don't want the sample effort to balloon and turn this into a data exercise before we've even aligned on the problem framing.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I think a 200-ticket sample will support the next phase, especially if it gives us enough coverage across the main support flows without slowing down discovery.

turns.inner_thought: If we start from the ML pilot label schema, I can organize the sample in a way that supports calibration and draft annotation instructions right away. Reusing prior artifacts only helps if they plug directly into downstream engineering work; otherwise we just recreate decisions later.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And if we reuse the pilot taxonomy to save time, it'll also make it easier for me to structure the sample and get the downstream guidance lined up.

turns.inner_thought: I should make the package look disciplined and complete enough to review, but it absolutely needs to preserve room for stakeholders to shape it. My baseline requirements package will be a coherent draft: goal statements, user scenarios, expected failure modes, constraints we already know, and the open questions I want architecture, legal, and support ops to react to. That's exactly what a good early review is for.
turns.utterance: On my side, the baseline requirements package will pull together the goal statements, core user scenarios, failure modes, and the open questions we want stakeholders to react to. That should give us a solid frame without overbuilding the document in week one.

turns.inner_thought: I want to reduce ambiguity before this goes in front of stakeholders. If I add feasibility notes now, architecture and legal can mostly validate the package in one pass rather than reopening foundational questions. Review should be confirmation, not another exploratory workshop.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I'll add feasibility notes before the stakeholder review so architecture and legal have enough context to validate the package in one pass.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle the interviews that help round out the framing and expose issues before review, but I'm still counting on the review itself to surface the gaps and disagreements we haven't found yet. That's the point of taking a reviewable package in early rather than waiting for everything to be settled.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll take the support-ops and customer-success interviews, and I'll fold that input into the package. The review should also help surface anything that's still ambiguous so we can tighten it after we get reactions.

turns.inner_thought: Once the baseline requirements are in, assuming the boundaries are stable, my team should be able to turn the sample and taxonomy into a durable labeling setup right away. With around 200 valid tickets per major bucket and the ML pilot taxonomy carried forward, we can start calibration without relabeling everything a week later.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Once the baseline requirements land, my team can start turning the sample and taxonomy into a stable labeling setup so implementation planning doesn't stall.

turns.inner_thought: Let me summarize this in a way that sounds crisp and executive-friendly: baseline requirements by Friday, 200-ticket sample in parallel, attach the routing taxonomy from the support-ops pilot, then review on Tuesday to get architecture, legal, and support ops shaping the package. If everyone nods, I can move fast without reopening process questions.
turns.utterance: Let me recap to make sure we're aligned: baseline requirements by Friday, the 200-ticket sample prepared in parallel, the pilot taxonomy attached, and then stakeholder review on Tuesday once it is ready. I'll own the interviews and package assembly, and you'll own the sample plus feasibility notes.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that timeline works. If Friday gives us the minimum stable requirements set I expect, and the sample and taxonomy are in place the way I'm planning, we should be able to move straight from Tuesday's review into implementation planning instead of circling back into requirement churn.
turns.utterance: Yep, that matches what I have. With those owners and timing, we should be in good shape to move into implementation planning right after the review.
